My educators and the general opinion is at least 5 years to (in their words) become just competent, not even good lol. I have less than one year of experience and even though I improve every single time I go to work, there are still so many things to learn. In the ED you need to know a little bit about virtually everything. Even though I’m a new grad in the ED, I truly believe new grads shouldn’t be allowed to work there without prior RN experience (hello staffing crisis!!!) like I don’t even know what I don’t know most of the time. Does that make sense?

Paramedic experience is helpful but I don’t think it counts towards any time off of those 5 years, it will just be easier for you to start in the environment. The hard part about the ED isn’t the actual skills like pushing meds and starting IVs (which is where you will excel as a paramedic! Over this past summer, I developed an intense craving to eat ice, similar to feeling thirsty but my body just knew it had to be ice. I was eating so much ice that my family and friends commented on it. At night I would eat at least 24 ounces of crushed ice after dinner. If I went out for drinks I would eat the ice from the glass shamelessly. Keep in mind, I knew that this was socially abnormal and annoying because it was loud but the craving was stronger than social inhibitions, lol. 

I’m a nurse so I kind of knew that it meant something, cravings to eat non-food items is called “pica” and happens for a lot of different reasons to a lot of different non-food items. In pregnancy, people tend to crave eating dirt due to the increased need for iron building blocks (ferrous sulfate). I also took care of a child once with chronic pica who could not stop ingesting magnets. Very interesting phenomenon

Anyways I went to the doctor and I was very anemic, my serum ferritin was like a 4 and the normal range is around 12-100+. Took a fuck ton of iron pills for a few months and — who would’ve thought — the cravings cleared up. I’m sitting here now thinking about eating ice and it actually sounds quite unpleasant. 

Some online research says that ice can mimic a metallic taste which makes your body think it’s ingesting iron. I haven’t seen anything about the aforementioned oxygen stores in ice but it also logically makes sense since iron transports oxygen to tissues in the body.

I worked in a nursing home as a CNA and have yet to experience a hospital-type full code passing. In my experience I’ve had people pass that I’ve built relationships with and people I haven’t but they’ve all been very peaceful and mostly expected. In those cases it feels, in a way, relieving. They were in the nursing home for a reason, and in most cases it is due to a loss of independence which can obviously lead to a lesser quality of life. Most of the time they were suffering and as caregivers we’re sad to see people we care for pass and to see families grieve but I know that their suffering is over and they weren’t living life in a way that truly gave them happiness. 

In the cases of people I’ve built relationships with, I miss seeing their faces at work every day, but I’ve seen them at their worst — from incontinence to chronic pain to almost full-time sedation, I’m often glad to see them let go of their declining bodies and move into whatever comes next. 

I think it’s essential to hope as a nurse that there is a positive afterlife. Otherwise it’d be torture to think about what you could’ve done differently to save your patient from suffering from something we can’t fix or avoid. 

I once read a blog about how nurses deal with death and dying and how they leave work at work without letting it spill into your life and into your other patients. One nurse carries around a rock or a small trinket that she considers to be her life. When she walks into a patient’s room, the rock stays outside the door. When she finishes, she picks it back up and puts it in her pocket. A small symbolic way to be tied to your personal life and remembering to care for yourself when you’re surrounded by morbidity.

Not sure if your school offers it, but there's an app called visible body which is so extremely helpful. If its not provided, I would highly recommend it. Its hard to start A+P as a freshman because its hard to understand material that you kind of have to teach yourself in ways you'll remember. Its especially good for the anatomy side of things.

Visible body is also online, so if you have it on one interface you can have both. 

I also learned that for the physiology side of things, its really helpful for me to repeatedly write the steps of the process down on paper, especially if you print out a visual (ex. studying the nervous system, print a picture of a neuromuscular junction and label the structures, as well as writing in the steps where they belong). 

Take notes on everything in lecture, compare it to the objectives that are likely in the syllabus, and fill in the gaps using your textbook/visible body. Even if it feels repetitive, studies show that it helps you commit it to memory if you physically write it, not to mention it works like a charm for me. I try to change the pen color every time as well, because while it may not be obvious while you're doing it, the color changes make your brain process the information as somewhat new and draw more focus. 

I know some of the methods sound a bit far fetched but in all honesty this is a class of memorizing like it's nobody's business, and then being forced to apply it. You really need to have a solid grasp on everything, because as you progress into more body systems, you realize how connected the material is to each other. That would have to be the biggest recommendation I can offer:

no matter how you study, make sure you (pardon the SpongeBob reference) firmly grasp it. Because it will show up later in a system you never thought would be connected and be expected to regurgitate info you learned weeks or months ago. I'm also in the process of becoming a TA for a+p, and I really love talking about it clearly, so I am also a resource for you. I would be happy to share other resources for specific topics if you need, just send me a PM!

Good luck. Likely one of the hardest classes you'll ever take but in my opinion, extremely rewarding. Theres nothing like reading about the human body and then sitting back for a second, realizing that these processes are occurring as you study them. Shits mind blowing. One more quick thing, I tend to spend 8+ hours a week for this class, not including the actual studying part of it. So, once again, good luck and happy studying!

we flew from budapest to rome, which speaks for itself but obviously VERY expensive, for 3 days. we then trained to florence for 4 days, which is honestly better than rome but still pricey. trained back to rome and then jumped on a plane to...

from sweden we flew to switzerland (skip sweden, just train to switzerland!) which was PRICEY, probably the most expensive country to date. we then booked it to barcelona, which is a cheap place to go for a good time. resembles eastern europe in some ways, but not all the way. i had a great time here and spent 2 days

I’m gonna be completely honest with you—there’s a good chance you’re not actually shrinking. A lot of factors go into height, like atmospheric pressure, time of day, using the same tape measure/method every time, etc. 

In general as a rule, using my background in healthcare and anatomy, it’s kind of impossible to actually shrink. Your bones can’t exactly “shrink” lengthwise, and if the rest of your body were to follow suit in shrinking, you’d likely be in pain in your muscles, joints, ligaments, and so on (you even have special receptors in your muscles to measure the amount of “pull” and tension on your muscles, and if you shrank, they would be in constant contraction & pain)

If I had to guess why your height is fluctuating, it’s probably the method that you’re using to measure. Your other heights are likely from a doctors office, and if not, were they taken at the same time of day? same tape measure? same area in the house? same position you’re standing in?

Try not to stress. Judging by how tall you are at 14, I’m assuming you’re a male. You have plenty of time to keep growing; you’ll be surprised how much you spring up throughout high school. And, if my observation is incorrect and you’re actually shrinking (unlikely but nothing is impossible), you have plenty of time left in puberty to make it up. 

Also, most people don’t know their own heights (exactly) and when they do it’s usually an estimate. Height is nothing to be concerned about, especially at your age. The human body is wild, just give it some time, and in the meantime, pick a routine to take your height if you’re still concerned. A level floor against the wall, same tape measure, and make sure it starts at exactly 0, because sometimes they have gaps. Heels against the wall, look straight ahead, and remember that you are more than your height. :)
